### ANNEX ON PERFORMANCE BY POLICY SECTORS

The Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) approved by the Government and the annual budget approved by the Parliament are the main documents that allocate public funds to achieve the objectives of the National Development Strategy (NDS), the Kosovo Economic Reform Program (KERP), the National Program for the Implementation of the Stabilization and Association Measures (NPISAM), and other strategic documents. Similar to other countries, Kosovo operates under conditions of limited resources, making it essential that every euro from collected public revenues is strategically allocated to activities that address the most pressing needs for the competitiveness of the economy and the well-being of the country's citizens.

To this end, the Government of Kosovo has approved the Public Financial Management Strategy with the strategic aim of improving the performance approach in the budget cycle. This is regulated by Article 21.l (paragraph l, point ii) of the Law on Public Financial Management and Responsibilities, which requires “a list of measurable objectives that are used to assess the success of a budget organization in fulfilling its mission.” This serves as information to enhance accountability and dialogue with legislators and citizens on policy issues.

This performance annex is divided into sixteen policy sectors. This approach is based on the international classification of COFOG (Classification of Government Functions) developed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which is used by all major international entities, such as the United Nations and the European Union, among many others.

Each sector in this annex is divided into three parts. The first part includes the objectives of the respective sector. The second part presents the objectives of the current budget cycle taken from the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework to establish a strategic link between the medium-term and annual budget perspectives. Finally, the third part of each sector presents the key measurable indicators.

At this stage, there are still no measurable values for some indicators due to the unavailability of reliable data.

### 1. PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION

1.1. Within this sector, the objectives are good governance, enhancing effectiveness and accountability, socio-economic development, advancing the country's integration processes, strengthening the international subjectivity of the Republic of Kosovo, and advancing and modernizing the entire public administration to serve efficiently, transparently, professionally, and impartially to all citizens, businesses, and the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating conditions for the sustainable return of displaced persons, protection, integration, and development of communities living in Kosovo.

1.2. The main objectives of this sector are:

          

Strengthening the international subjectivity of the Republic of Kosovo and implementing criteria in the process of integration into the EU and international institutions;

Modernizing public administration as well as strengthening integrity and institutional development;

The return and reintegration in Kosovo and the construction of the necessary infrastructure for the normal functioning of returnees;

Stabilizing communities and closing collective centers in Kosovo;

Preventing and combating corruption through preventive mechanisms for asset declaration, conflict of interest, and whistleblowing;

Increasing quality in policy development and service delivery for citizens and businesses;

Enhancing interoperability for national security, consolidating, and strengthening the security sector center;

Sustainable and balanced regional development and increasing inter-municipal and crossborder cooperation;

Promoting and protecting human rights and ensuring gender equality through women's empowerment, as well as promoting and protecting the rights of communities;

Increasing foreign investments and exports through the functionalization of the Kosovo Agency for Investments and Exports;

Documenting and researching crimes committed during the war.

### 2. PUBLIC FINANCE

2.1 The main aim within this sector is the sustainability and management of public finances in accordance with the strategic framework and obligations under the European integration agenda, as well as ensuring the implementation of priorities in maintaining fiscal discipline to preserve macro-fiscal stability that guarantees sustainability and economic growth. The advancement of fiscal policies will be oriented to ensure support and fair treatment of economic entities, increase tax revenues and formal employment, as well as intensify efforts to eliminate tax evasion, combat the informal economy, and fight against money laundering. Additionally, there is a goal for greater engagement in increasing the efficiency and effectiveness of public procurement, strengthening electronic procurement, as well as increasing the transparency of public tenders, to achieve a fair ratio between value and expenditure.

2.2 The main objectives of this sector are:



      

Harmonization of legislation in the field of Public Finances in accordance with the obligations arising from the Stabilization and Association Agreement (SAA) and international standards;

Ensuring the implementation of fiscal discipline to maintain macro-fiscal stability;

Increasing allocative efficiency in public money management to provide quality services to citizens;

Increasing operational efficiency in public money management, in accordance with applicable rules and standards;

Ensuring sound public finances through reforms in Public Financial Management and cooperation with International Financial Institutions;

Reducing tax evasion, the informal economy, and money laundering;

Advancing the electronic procurement system, increasing efficiency and effectiveness, as well as transparency in public tenders, ensuring equal treatment and value for money;

A transparent and digitized system for managing public finances.

2.3. Key Performance Indicators Key Performance Indicators

3% (2022)

19%

### 3. FOREIGN POLICY AND INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS

3.1 Within this sector, the aim is to formulate and implement the foreign policy of the Republic of Kosovo, protect Kosovo's interests in relation to other countries and international organizations, represent Kosovo abroad, preserve and protect the immunities and privileges of diplomatic missions and the individuals entitled to them according to international conventions and customs, and develop and coordinate policies in relation to other countries. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora defends and promotes the national, cultural, and economic policies of the Republic of Kosovo. Regarding the diaspora, Kosovo will treat it as an extraordinary potential in promoting the image of Kosovo and will advance the protection of the rights and interests of Kosovo citizens abroad. Currently, the primary priority of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora is membership in international organizations and increasing recognitions of the Republic of Kosovo.

3.2 The main objectives of this sector are:

    

Creating and strengthening bilateral relations with other countries;

Strengthening regional cooperation;

Kosovo's membership in international and regional organizations;

Strengthening Diaspora Diplomacy;

Strengthening Public Diplomacy and Economic Diplomacy.

3.3. Key Performance Indicators

Key Performance Indicators

### 4. PROTECTION AND SECURITY

4.1. Within this sector, the aim is to draft and implement general state policies in the field of defense according to the applicable legislation. The competencies and functions of the Ministry of Defense are defined by the existing laws. The Kosovo Security Force is a multiethnic, professional, armed military force authorized to serve both domestically and abroad, in accordance with the constitutional and legal powers granted for the protection of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Kosovo, supporting civil authorities, and participating in international operations. The Ministry of Defense and the Kosovo Security Force will focus on: harmonizing and fulfilling the objectives set in strategic documents; unifying and realizing the planningprogramming, budgeting, and execution process; fulfilling obligations specified in the Comprehensive Transition Plan; consolidating the education and training system; consolidating the system for cyber defense; and increasing the skill levels of KSF units to contribute to operations both domestically and abroad.

4.2. The main objectives of this sector are:

     

Development of military capacities for the protection of sovereignty and territorial integrity;

Strengthening civil democratic oversight and increasing accountability and transparency;

Expanding bilateral cooperation, membership in organizations, and participation in international operations;

Maintaining essential capabilities to support civil authorities;

Completing and advancing the legal framework in the field of defense;

Advancing inter-state cooperation to gain access to inter-state and international programs for military equipment and purchases in the fields of security and defense.

4.3. Key Performance Indicators Key Performance Indicators

Baseline level (year)

Membership in regional initiatives, PfP, and NATO integration

### 5. PUBLIC SECURITY

5.1. The mission of the Public Security Sector is to uphold the rule of law, public safety throughout the territory of the Republic of Kosovo, and to prepare public policies in accordance with the Constitution and applicable legislation. This mission aims to ensure an independent, impartial, and professional system for advancing the legislative and strategic framework. Within this sector, the Strategy for the Prevention and Combating of Terrorism, the Cyber Security Strategy, the National Response Plan, and the Disaster Risk Reduction Strategy have been approved.

5.2. The main objectives of this sector are:

 Improvement of public safety;

 Advancement of policies and functionalization of mechanisms for Cyber Security;

 Building professional capacities of public security institutions through standardized training programs;

 Prevention and combatting of organized crime, corruption, and terrorism, as well as efficient management of migration and border control;

 Continuous improvement of the capacities of the Intelligence Agency to avert global security threats to national security.

High readiness for response and emergencies Combatting crime and corruption Reduction in the number of accidents

### 6. JUSTICE

6.1. The mission of the Justice Sector is to prepare public policies, legal and sub-legal acts, and mandatory standards in the field of Justice in accordance with the Constitution and applicable legislation, as well as to ensure an independent, impartial, professional, and effective prosecutorial and judicial system. The Ministry of Justice, as the bearer of the Justice sector, is committed to ensuring that the state of Kosovo is a state of law and the rule of law. The Ministry of Justice will show special commitment to forming a sustainable legal system that will be fair, swift, efficient, and will strengthen citizens' trust in the country’s institutions and the justice system as a whole.

6.2. The main objectives of this sector are:



      

Investigation and prosecution of offenders of criminal acts reflecting professionalism, dedication, efficiency, and full respect for human rights and freedoms through the implementation of the highest professional and ethical standards;

Development and implementation of policies to ensure fair and effective access to the justice system for all community members in accordance with applicable legislation;

Functional review of the Justice Sector;

Combatting organized crime and corruption;

Development and implementation of policies for social and family services as well as child protection;

Protection and supervision of the fundamental human rights and freedoms through the increased influence of the Institution of the Ombudsman;

Prevention and combatting of domestic violence, violence against women, and genderbased violence;

Exercising responsibilities in the search, retrieval, securing, and verification of information related to the location and fate of missing persons and the return of the remains of missing persons.

6.3. Key Performance Indicators Key Performance Indicators

### 7. ENVIRONMENT

7.1. Within this sector, the aim is to monitor and protect the environment, water, as well as the development and strengthening of spatial planning, construction, housing, cadastre, and expropriation at the national level. Kosovo faces problems with water management, waste, air, and soil pollution. Other environmental issues arise from unplanned spatial developments and unauthorized constructions that damage the environment and reduce opportunities for future development of the country. Kosovo aims to pursue a Green Agenda as an important element around the principles of an economy centered on the environment, defined by sustainable growth, sustainable consumption of resources, and reduction of carbon emissions.

7.2. The main objectives of this sector are:

 Completion of the legal infrastructure in the field of the environment and its harmonization with EU legislation and its implementation;

 Improvement of the state of the environment and monitoring its status;

 Creation of an efficient administrative system for spatial planning, construction, housing, energy efficiency in buildings, and cadastre;

 Better administration and management of water resources and rehabilitation of riverbeds and waste management;

 

Strengthening of the environmental, water, nature, spatial planning, housing, and construction inspectorates;

Advancement of tariff policies, raising the standards of water service, and reducing water losses.

### MACRO-FISCAL FRAMEWORK 2026-2028

\1. World Economy

The global economy continues to face a period of considerable uncertainty and slow economic growth. According to the latest estimates, world GDP is expected to grow by 3.2% in 2025 and

3.1% in 2026, indicating a slowdown compared to 3.3% in 2024. These forecasts are much lower compared to the pre-pandemic average, reflecting a new landscape marked by protectionism, policy uncertainty and fragmentation. The October forecasts compared to July show very little change, while compared to April forecasts, when tariff shocks triggered a sharp downward revision, the current outlook reflects a modest improvement due to lower effective tariff rates and easing financial conditions. However, the trajectory remains significantly below the optimistic forecasts of late 2024, before the implementation of trade protectionist measures.

The US economy is projected to grow by 2.0% in 2025 and 2.1% in 2026, while the Eurozone countries are projected to grow by 1.2% and 1.1% respectively. Over the medium term (20252030), the world economy is projected to expand at an average annual rate of 3.2%. This belowhistorical performance reflects structural imbalances including aging populations, weak productivity growth, trade fragmentation and high policy uncertainty.

Trade policy uncertainty remains high despite some tariff reductions since the April peaks, with effective tariff rates between 10-20% imposed by the US on most countries. Supply chain disruptions, technological disconnection and limitations on knowledge diffusion threaten longterm productivity. Immigration restrictions in advanced economies reduce labor supply, particularly affecting sectors dependent on migrant workers. Official development assistance cuts are negatively affecting low-income countries. In addition, unfavorable fiscal prospects, high debt burdens and limited policy space constrain the ability of governments in developing countries to support economic growth.

Global inflation is projected to decline from 5.8% in 2024 to 4.2% in 2025 and 3.7% in 2026.

However, there is considerable variation across regions, with inflation expectations remaining high in some emerging markets and moderate in others. Advanced economies are expected to see inflation decline from 2.6% in 2024 to 2.5% in 2025 and 2.2% in 2026, moving closer to central bank targets. The United States is facing rising inflationary pressures, with inflation projected at 2.7% in 2025 before easing to 2.4% in 2026. Emerging economies face higher inflation, projected at 5.3% in 2025 and 4.7% in 2026, significantly lower than the 7.9% inflation seen in 2024. Disinflation has been stronger than expected in some Asian economies, while inflation in Brazil and Mexico has been revised upward due to currency pressures and sustained services sector inflation. Core inflation has risen in the United States as the impact of tariffs has been passed on to consumer prices.

Central banks are facing divergent policy trajectories. Monetary policy must maintain a balance between price stability and promoting economic growth, with central bank independence remaining a key factor in stabilizing inflation expectations in the face of political pressures.

Financial markets remain accommodative by historical standards, despite recent periods of volatility. A temporary risk episode in early August 2025, triggered by the weak US jobs report, caused global stock indices to decline, but these movements quickly reversed, marking one of the fastest recoveries in history. The rapid rise of stablecoins, as alternatives to traditional assets and bank deposits, could encourage currency substitution. In the event of a sudden flow to a given stablecoin, this could jeopardize the market for underlying assets such as short-term government bonds or demand deposits, which could pose systemic risks to the stability of the financial system.

Fiscal policy remains very accommodative in major economies despite high debt levels.

Although the primary deficits projected for 2025 are in most cases lower than the record deficits of 2020-2021, when large fiscal stimulus packages were implemented to fight the shocks of the pandemic, they remain significantly higher than in the pre-pandemic period. Calculating debt sustainability after the pandemic has become more complex due to high debt ratios, deteriorating primary balances, higher interest rates and weakening growth prospects. In many countries, there is an urgent need to move towards fiscal consolidation in order to ensure stabilization of debt dynamics and rebuild much-needed fiscal buffers. Gradual reductions in monetary policy rates provide fiscal relief by reducing financing costs, but this will not be sufficient, especially in cases where long-term real interest rates still remain high.

\2. Recent Economic Developments in Kosovo The year 2024 was characterized by a stable economic growth of 4.6% in real terms and 6.9% in nominal terms, while inflation marked a slowdown trend, reaching 1.6%. According to data from KAS, the growth of economic activity has continued in the first half of 2025. During the first half of 2025, economic growth in real terms is 3.8%, while in nominal terms it is 5.8%.

This growth was mainly driven by consumption, which recorded an increase of 6.5% in real terms and contributed 6.7 pp to GDP growth.

Total investments (private and public) in the first half of 2025 increased by 9.0% compared to the first half of 2024, making a positive contribution of 3.1 pp to GDP growth.

On the other hand, net exports in the first half of 2025 increased by 16.2%, with a negative contribution of .6.0 pp. Exports increased by 11.1% (exports of goods decreased by 4.7%, while exports of services increased by 16.9%) with a contribution to economic growth of 4.1 pp (exports of goods had a negative contribution of 0.5 pp, while exports of services had a positive contribution of 4.5 pp).

Imports increased by 13.7% (15.3% imports of goods and 7.1% imports of services) with a negative contribution of 10.0 pp (goods by 9.00 pp and services by 1.0 pp).

Inflation - measured through the harmonized consumer price index - increased by 3.4% on average in the period January-September 2025. The categories that had the most growth were:

the 'food and non-alcoholic beverages' with an increase of 7.3%, the 'restaurants and hotels'

with an increase of 6.1%, the 'alcoholic beverages and tobacco' with an increase of 4.8%, while the 'transport' and 'communication' categories recorded a decrease of 2.3% and 1.8% respectively.

The current account deficit during the January-July period amounted to -742.2 million euros, a significant increase of about 38.5% compared to the same period last year.

The trade deficit in goods continued to expand by around 19.0% during this period. Meanwhile, the surplus in services recorded a significant annual increase of 22.2%.

Exports of goods decreased by 1.6%, while exports of services increased by 13.6% annually.

According to the latest data on the structure of goods exports, exports of the category 'prepared food items, beverages and tobacco' increased compared to the same period last year, increasing their participation in total exports from 10.6% last year to 12.4% during the January-July period of this year. While the category 'base metals and articles thereof' marked a decrease of 8.7%, marking a decrease in its participation in total exports (23.4% from 25.2% last year), the category 'other manufactured articles' also marked a decrease of 10.2% and its participation in total exports (10.4% from 11.4% last year); the category 'mineral products' also marked a decrease in exports by 11.8%, constituting about 6.1% of total exports. Regarding the contribution of the categories to the decrease in the export of goods, the export of 'base metals and articles thereof' had the most pronounced impact with -2.2 pp, and 'other manufactured articles' with -1.2 pp. The export of services has marked an increase of 22.2% compared to the same period last year. This increase came mainly from the increase in travel services with a contribution of 11.3 pp, computer, information and telecommunication services with 1.9 pp and transport with a contribution of 0.7 pp, while the 'construction' category marked a negative contribution of 0.4 pp.

Imports of goods marked an increase of 14.8% compared to the previous year, mainly driven by the category 'mineral products' with an increase of 23.5% and a contribution of 3.2 pp, 'transport vehicles' with an increase of 22.2% and a positive contribution of 2.6 pp, 'imports of machinery, tools, electrical equipment' with an increase of 15.3% and a contribution of 1.8 pp

and 'prepared food, beverages and tobacco' with an increase of 11.0% and a contribution of 1.3 pp. Meanwhile, imports of services marked an increase of 4.5%, mainly driven by a significant increase in imports of transport services with a contribution of 4.2 pp, and the category of travel services with 1.7 pp and 'pension and insurance services' with a contribution of 1.5 pp. This increase was offset by the decline in the categories 'Other business services', 'Fees for the use of intellectual property' and 'Computer, information and telecommunications services' with a negative contribution of 1.7pp, 0.7pp and 0.5pp.

Bank loans have continued to be a stable source of financing for the economy.

At the end of August 2025, the loan stock reached a value of around 6.4 billion euros, marking an increase of 17.7% compared to the previous year. The stock of corporate loans has increased by 14.5%, while the stock of household loans has increased by 21.5%.

Deposits continued their growth, with the main contribution from households. At the end of August 2025, the stock of total deposits reached a value of around 7.3 billion euros, thus marking an annual increase of 12.9%. The stock of corporate deposits increased by 13.4% while that of households by 12.7%. Regarding the type of deposits, transferable deposits recorded an annual increase of 11.6% and contributed to the increase in total deposits by 0.07 pp. The level of non-performing loans (NPLs) reached 2.1% at the end of August 2025, meaning there is no change from the same period last year (2.1%). The average weighted interest rate on loans during the period January-August 2025 reached 6.7%, from 6.1% in the same period last year. Meanwhile, the weighted average interest rate on deposits fluctuated around 3.0%, from 2.9%, which was the average during the same period last year.

\3. Macroeconomic Outlook According to MFPT estimates, Kosovo's economy is expected to grow by around 4.3 % in real terms and 7.8% in nominal terms. Based on the latest data from KAS Kosovo's economy has continued its growth trend.

The expectation for an average real economic growth of 4.3% in 2025 shows a downward revision of 1.3 percentage points compared to the previous round of projections conducted in April 2025, mainly as a result of the downward revision of the contribution of all components.

The Consumer Price Index is expected to fluctuate around 3.6% during 2025, remaining higher than the level recorded in 2024 (1.6%). The inflation performance has been determined by the price performance in international food, energy and oil markets due to geopolitical tensions.

After moderate growth during the current year, Kosovo's economy is expected to grow at a faster pace next year (2026), estimated at around 4.9% in real terms and 7.7% in nominal terms.

Unlike 2025, the main contribution to economic growth in 2026 is expected to come from private consumption, exports of services and private investments. Public investments are expected to have the same execution dynamics as a result of the continuation of existing projects and the implementation of a number of projects within the framework of the growth plan. The increase in the minimum wage, the continued growth of bank loans, although at a slower rate than the current year, as well as the increase in a number of social transfers (for maternity and social assistance) will continue to support the growth of private consumption in the coming year, while remittances will also continue to maintain their historical growth trend.

Meanwhile, public consumption will increase due to the increase in the wage bill in the public sector and the increase in spending on government goods and services.

Exports of goods and services will continue their positive contribution, but to a higher extent compared to 2025 (with differences between the contribution of goods and services) mainly due to the base effect, increased exports of goods and the stabilization of prices of basic goods in international markets.

Imports of goods and services will continue their upward trend, with the main factors for this growth being the increase in capital investments and the increase in travel services.

Over the next year (2026), based on expectations of commodity prices in international markets, inflation in Kosovo is expected to be reduced to 2.8% and further stabilize around an average of 2.0% in the medium term.

However, the baseline projection of inflation and economic growth is surrounded by downside risks, related to further increases in core prices in international markets, slowing economic growth in trading partner countries, or developments that may occur in Kosovo's energy sector.

\4. Government revenues and expenditures

4.1 Revenues and Expenditures January-September 2025

According to preliminary data for the first nine months of 2025, both budget revenues and expenditures have increased compared to the same period of the previous year. Specifically, budget revenues (including DDGs) have reached the amount of 2,493.1 million euros, which represents an increase of 10.1% compared to January-September 2024. At the same time, budget expenditures (including DDGs) have recorded the value of 2,256.7 million euros, with an increase of 12.8%. If we compare them with the projections for the reporting period, revenues have achieved a higher rate of realization than expenditures. As a result of the flow of revenues and expenditures, the overall budget balance recorded a surplus of 236.4 million euros for this period.

Revenues from direct taxes increased by about 9.0% on an annual basis during the period January-September 2025, reaching the amount of 425.8 million Euros. This increase was helped, among other things, by the increase in the number of employees in the private sector as well as the increase in salaries in both the private and public sectors. Regarding the types of direct taxes, revenues from personal income tax increased by about 7.4% compared to the same period last year, while corporate income tax increased by 8.6%. It is worth noting that property tax has decreased by 24.0% during this period.

The increase in the value of imported goods has directly driven the significant increase in indirect tax revenues. For the period January-September 2025, based on customs data, regular imports increased by 13.8%. During this period, indirect tax revenues reached the value of 1,836.5 million Euros, marking an increase of 10.0% compared to January-September 2024.

Border VAT revenues increased by 10.1% in annual terms, while customs duties recorded an increase of 11.2%. Excise duties, as one of the main sources of indirect revenues, also recorded an upward trend with a rate of 4.2% for the reporting period.

Throughout the relevant period, non-tax revenues reached the value of 260.4 million Euros, which represents an increase of 1.5% compared to the previous year. Of the categories of nontax revenues, the concession tax marked an increase of 29.0% and local level revenues by

22.5%. On the other hand, central level revenues recorded a decrease of 15.9%.

For the period January-September 2025, budget expenditures increased in all categories. The category of wages and salaries has marked an annual increase of 5.3%. Expenditures for goods and services also increased by 18.3%, reaching the value of 333.5 million Euros. Subsidies and transfers were also characterized by an increase of 15.0% compared to the same period of 2024.

Capital expenditures marked a significant increase of 19.9% during the period JanuarySeptember 2025 compared to the previous year. Regarding the financing structure of capital expenditures during this period, the regular budget prevailed with about 84.2%, followed by

own-source revenues with 8.1%, external borrowing financed by the investment clause with

3.1%, own-source revenues carried over from the previous year with 3.0% and revenues from financing from regular borrowings with 1.7%.

Interest Expennditures during the January-September period reached 37.8 million euros, marking an annual increase of 16.8%.

4.2 Revenue forecast for 2026 and the medium term

Budget revenues are expected to increase by around 7.9 % over the medium-term period, mainly as a result of the continuation of measures taken by the Government, voluntary compliance and the formalization of the economy.

Revenues from indirect taxes will continue to have the highest share in total revenues, with around 74.4% in 2026 and are expected to increase by around 11.4% compared to the 2025 Budget.

Revenues from direct taxes during 2025 are expected to increase by around 11.3% compared to the 2025 Budget and constitute 17.9% of total revenues.

Non-tax revenues during 2026 are expected to record a slight increase of 0.2% compared to the budget law for 2025, reaching the amount of approximately 357.7 million Euros.

Grants for 2026 are expected to reach a value of 22.5 million Euros, the same level as the previous year.

In the period 2027-2028, total budget revenues are expected to increase by an average of

7.9%. Direct taxes in the period 2027-2028 are expected to have an average increase of 8.3%;

indirect taxes are expected to have an average increase of 7.3%, and non-tax revenues are expected to follow their historical trend with an average increase of 4.0%.

4.3 Expenditure forecast for the period 2026 and the medium term

Total budget expenditures in 2026 are expected to increase by 9.9% in annual terms, compared to the 2025 Budget. The greatest impact on the increase in budget expenditures is from the measures taken by the Government to increase the well-being of citizens.

Total Current Expenditures during 2026 are planned to increase by 10.7% compared to the 2025 Budget, reaching 2,893.9 million Euros.

Expenditures for the category of wages and salaries are planned to be 980.4 million Euros and to mark an increase of 6.9%, staying within the fiscal rule. This increase comes as a result of the increase in the number of employees. Expenditures in the category of goods and services are planned to remain at the same level, marking a modest increase of 1.6% compared to the Budget for 2025. Subsidies and transfers during 2026 are expected to increase by

17.4%. This increase is mainly due to the increase in pensions, maternity benefits and the increase in social assistance. While 10 million Euros have been allocated to the current reserve category.

Capital expenditures are expected to increase by 7.2% in 2026, reaching a share of 25.5% of total expenditures. During this period, the implementation of capital projects is expected based on a list of priorities that includes projects with an impact on improving the transport network, improving the electricity network and improving conditions in education, social and health systems. The majority of capital investments are expected to be financed from the regular budget, but a large number of projects in different sectors are planned to be financed from external borrowing through the investment clause.

Upward revision of budget expenditures by about 83.5 million Euros:



Increase in current expenditures by approximately 95.0 million euros as a result of the implementation of Government decisions to increase social assistance and the value of maternity benefits.

 Lower capital expenditures by about 18 million euros.

State Financing and Borrowing

borrowing from the internal market through Securities, (b) obtaining loans from financial institutions international; (c) In 2026, no income from the liquidation funds is expected. During 2026, the bank balance is estimated to be around 3.0% of the GDP forecast for this year.

Transfers may decide to issue a lower amount of domestic debt compared to the amount of domestic debt forecast in Table 1 of this law.

### FISCAL RISK STATEMENT

Overview Fiscal risk is the exposure of public finances to uncertain or unforeseen events that could cause actual fiscal outcomes to deviate from projected forecasts. These risks can arise from various sources such as unexpected developments in the global or domestic economy, changing conditions in financial or commodity markets or natural disasters and public health emergencies. Additionally, longer-term fiscal risks and spending pressures typically emerge from climate change and can also arise from changes in the population and age-profile of the labour force.

Managing fiscal risks requires a better understanding of the nature, likelihood, and impact of such factors. The management of fiscal risk, along with its integration into fiscal planning and budget preparation, has become increasingly prevalent around the world.

This Fiscal Risk Statement (FRS) provides a summary of potential risks and uncertainties that could affect Kosovo’s economy, presenting how their materialization might disrupt the baseline fiscal projections and expectations for the medium term, potentially leading to significant deviations from anticipated fiscal outcomes. As demonstrated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the materialization of such fiscal risks can impose significant financial costs on the economy, highlighting the necessity of identifying, analyzing, reporting, and managing them.

In some areas, the FRS focuses primarily on monitoring available data, serving as a tool to keep track of evolving risks.

The report is structured into two main sections: (1) an analysis of macroeconomic risks, primarily originating from the external environment, and an evaluation of budget performance;

and (2) a review of specific fiscal risks. In line with the previous version, it includes an analysis on Kosovo’s debt, on-lending, guarantees, public-private partnerships, an evaluation of the performance of public-owned enterprises, and an overview of the financial sector's resilience.

This document presents both qualitative discussions of key risks and, where feasible, quantitative analysis.

This statement will be updated on a regular basis and published as an annex to the macro-fiscal framework of the Law on Budgetary Allocation and the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework.

The drafting and publication of this Statement aim to enhance fiscal transparency and assist policy makers to better understand the nature and magnitude of fiscal risks in order to put in place the appropriate policies to prevent or mitigate the consequences in case of their materialization.

Fiscal risks The fiscal risks included in this Statement are classified as high, medium or low risk, using the IMF analytical tool (FRAT: Fiscal Risk Assessment Tool)1, based on two criteria: the impact of fiscal risk and the likelihood of the risk materializing. Table 1 below specifies the criteria to categorize and prioritize fiscal risks based on their likelihood of occurring.

Over the medium term, the fiscal impact and likelihood of materialization of risks for PublicPrivate Partnerships, Debt, On-lending, and Guarantees are expected to remain low.

Nevertheless, the interconnectedness of the sectors, could amplify risk exposure.

Due to growing uncertainties in the international and domestic environment, compared to the classification on FRS in the Law on Budgetary Allocation for 2025, Macro-economic risks have shifted to a medium likelihood of materialization. Risks related to Public Enterprises are

also expected to maintain a medium level of fiscal impact and likelihood of materialization over the medium term Therefore, both macroeconomic risks and risks from Public Enterprises should continue to be closely and consistently monitored to ensure timely mitigation if needed.

Macro-Fiscal risks

2.1.1 Macroeconomic Risks The baseline framework presented in the Budget Law (Budget Appropriations for the Budget of the Republic of Kosovo) is, as every year, accompanied by risks that may negatively affect the macro-fiscal outlook, depending on the probability of their materialization and the intensity with which these risks occur. For the sake of careful planning and in the interest of transparency, the macro-fiscal framework will also take these risks into account, the details of which will be provided below.

As can be seen in a scenario where inflation increases by 0.5 percentage points (p.p.), GDP growth is expected to slow down to 4.3% in 2026, 4.6% in 2027, and 5.4% in 2028 demonstrating that elevated inflation hinders economic performance. Conversely, a 10percentage point shortfall in capital expenditure implementation produces a more moderate effect on real GDP growth rates. Overall, both higher inflation and under-execution of CAPEX lead to slower GDP growth, with inflation having a more pronounced effect.

Risks from the Domestic Environment Increase in energy prices – The 16.1%2 increase in regulated electricity tariffs approved in April 2025 represents only the initial layer of energy sector risks threatening Kosovo's economic outlook. The market liberalization implemented in June 2025, requiring businesses with over 50 employees or €10 million annual turnover to purchase electricity on the open market, has exposed firms to substantial price increases that will likely be passed on to consumers, intensifying inflationary pressures. These developments are compounded by profound structural vulnerabilities: Kosovo's energy market remains over 90% dependent on two aging coal-fired power plants (Kosovo A and Kosovo B) that frequently experience supply shortages, forcing costly imports at a time when European electricity prices remain elevated following the crisis in Ukraine. This combination of higher tariffs, market uncertainty, and supply constraints poses significant downside risks to near-term GDP growth through reduced consumer purchasing power, elevated business costs, and potential disruptions to industrial

https://www.ero-ks.org/zrre/sites/default/files/Publikimet/Vendimet/Vendimet%202025/V_2703_2025.pdf

production. Over the longer term, however, sustained higher energy costs could catalyse a beneficial transition, encouraging firms and consumers to adopt energy-efficient technologies, renewable sources, and alternative fuels, an investment-intensive shift that may ultimately reshape production processes, enhance energy security, and support more sustainable economic growth.

Further tightening of the labour market – Kosovo's labor market, particularly for lowskilled and certain skilled positions, has experienced notable tightening since the pandemic.

This trend differs from many developed countries but shares similarities with regional developments in the Western Balkans. Several factors have contributed to this shift: the uneven pace of post-pandemic economic recovery, significant outward migration of working-age population following the 2024 visa liberalization with the European Union, demographic challenges including youth emigration, and evolving labour supply-demand dynamics driven by remittance-dependent consumption patterns and the informal economy. This tightening has been reflected in wage pressures in specific sectors, though comprehensive data from the Tax Administration of Kosovo (TAK) show an 11.2% increase in wages over the past three years.

Over the medium term considered in this Fiscal Risk Statement, continued labour market tightening, despite potential positive effects such as wage increases in certain sectors and possible productivity improvements, presents significant challenges, including: labour shortages in key industries (particularly construction, hospitality, and healthcare), persistent skills mismatches between educational output and market needs, and potential constraints on foreign direct investment due to labour availability concerns. These challenges require comprehensive policy interventions, including reforms to vocational training systems, incentives for diaspora engagement, further efforts on the formalization of the informal economy, and strategic workforce development planning to ensure sustainable economic growth.

Risks from the External Environment Volatility of commodity prices in international markets – Commodity prices are now projected to decline significantly in 2025 and further in 2026. However, commodity markets remain highly volatile, with sharp price fluctuations observed through 2025 alone. There are still potential sources that could push prices beyond baseline projections. The possible tariffs by the United States will contribute to global inflationary pressures, leading to lower overall productivity, weaker economic activity, and higher production costs and prices. All these factors create ongoing price uncertainties, especially for import-dependent developing countries like Kosovo.

Monetary policy in the eurozone – The ECB has maintained interest rates steady at 2.0% (deposit facility rate) since July 2025, following eight rate cuts since June 2024. The ECB is following a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach amid heightened uncertainty from trade tensions. The tightening of monetary policy by Eurozone countries, particularly key trading partners of Kosovo where a large portion of the Kosovar diaspora resides, continues to weigh on their economic activity, which could negatively affect remittances and spillover into Kosovo's economy. While Kosovo's exposure to foreign currency debt remains limited,

keeping risks from currency fluctuations relatively insignificant, the overall economic slowdown in these countries poses indirect risks.

Weakening economic activity in developed European countries – A slowdown in Eurozone economy, driven by elevated uncertainty from U.S. tariffs, weak manufacturing activity, and subdued business confidence, would be reflected in reduced exports and remittances to Kosovo, leading to slower economic activity, lower budget revenues, and potentially rising prices, particularly for food items.

Geopolitical tensions – A further escalation of the war in Ukraine and the emergence of new conflict hotspots could lead to additional disruptions in global supply chains, affecting global trade and especially energy markets. This could result in increased prices for food, energy, and oil.

As is the case with other interconnected economies, Kosovo faces growing vulnerabilities from both domestic and external risks that weigh on overall economic stability, consumption, and investment. Their estimated effects are incorporated into the baseline projections, while the sensitivity analysis, shown in Table 2 above, accounts for potentially larger or unforeseen shocks.

Total budget revenues, for January–September 2025 slightly exceeded projections, reaching

102.2% of the plan. Tax revenues amounted to 102.2% of the projection, driven by indirect taxes (103.3%) while direct taxes underperformed and non-tax revenues were marginally below target. A substantial increase in grant realization was recorded compared to the previous year (36.4% in 2024 vs. 154.3% in 2025). This over performance primarily reflects the delayed disbursement of grants initially planned for the prior year. Nevertheless, given that grants constitute roughly 1% of total budget revenues, their volatility is assessed as having limited fiscal relevance.

On the expenditure side, total budget expenditures were under executed at 95.49% of the budget, an improvement relative to January – September 2024 (91%). Current expenditures exceeded projections at 102.6% (up from 97.7% in 2024), in part due to higher salary-related outlays, whereas capital expenditures remained below plan at 72.4%, but saw an improvement from 66.9% in 2024. The continued under execution of capital projects, particularly loanfinanced projects pose a downside risk to growth and revenue forecasts. To accelerate the implementation of IFI-financed projects, the Ministry of Finance, Labor, and Transfers (MFLT) has begun ensuring that technical assessments and project documentation are completed prior to the signing of the respective financial agreements.

Payments from legal claims Payments related to the settlement of legal claims represent another form of unexpected expenditure that can pose fiscal risks. These payments, often arising from court rulings or contractual disputes, can be substantial and difficult to predict.

Specific Risks

2.2.1. Fiscal Risks from Debt, On-lending and Guarantees Debt plays an important role in government financing, but if not managed carefully, it can significantly impact the fiscal stance by increasing interest costs, limiting budgetary flexibility, and heightening vulnerability to economic shocks and refinancing risks.

To ensure fiscal stability, the Law on State Debt and State Guarantees sets a debt ceiling of 40% of GDP, including state guarantees, and imposes limits on municipal borrowing, requiring government (MoF) approval. The State Debt Program (SDP) also sets risk limits to manage:

  

Refinancing Risk: No more than 50% of domestic debt should mature within a year, and the average maturity must exceed 1 year.

Exchange Rate Risk: Foreign currency debt must not exceed 30% of total debt.

Interest Rate Risk: Floating interest rate debt must not exceed 30% of total debt.

Overview Public debt remains sustainable and posseses low risk to fiscal sustainability. The Debt-to-GDP ratio (Figure 5) has declined from 16.91% in 2024 to 15.98% by June 2025, well below the 40% fiscal rule, driven by lower domestic borrowing and guarantees.

Nevertheless, POEs continue to represent a potential risk, as they hold strategic importance, especially in delivering necessary services to the public, and as such it is expected from the government to act as an implicit “guarantor”, and help POEs in times of difficulties to ensure the continuing of essential services. For a more detailed analysis of the financial performance of POEs, see the section on POEs.

As of January–June 2025, on-lending, in the Treasury’s semi-annual report, represents 0.4% of GDP. The majority of on-lending is directed toward the energy sector (POEs), with all financing sourced from multilateral institutions such as KfW, EBRD, and IDA. These risks are closely tied to the financial performance of the enterprises, necessitating continuous monitoring. A deterioration in their financial condition could create medium-term fiscal risks for the government, not only through increased subsidies for the services provided, but also through the potential materialization of contingent liabilities associated with these on-lending arrangements. However, since on-lending represents only around 0.4% of GDP, the fiscal impact of these risks materializing is limited.

Rollover risk (refinancing), measured by the average time to maturity (ATM), has decreased in Kosovo, with ATM rising from 5.5 years in 2022 to 5.9 years in 2024. This reflects a reduced need for short-term refinancing, supported by long-maturity, low-interest concessional external loans, and a decreasing share of debt maturing within one year.

Interest rate risk remains low, as 91.6% of total debt is fixed-rate and only 8.4% is floating, mainly from IMF budget support and EBRD loans. Although floating-rate debt has increased slightly from 5.8% in 2023 to 8.3% in 2024, overall exposure is limited.

In terms of currency exposure, 91.3% of Kosovo’s total state debt in 2024 is denominated in euros, with only 8.7% in foreign currencies. This composition is expected to remain stable over the medium term, maintaining exchange rate risk at manageable levels.

Debt Sustainability Analysis Debt Sustainability Analysis 4(DSA) is a critical tool for assessing Kosovo's ability to meet its debt obligations while maintaining fiscal stability and supporting economic growth. The analysis is grounded in macroeconomic assumptions, including robust nominal growth averaging 8.0% from 2025 to 2027, before stabilizing at around 4.0%, and continued adherence to the fiscal rule, which limits the budget deficit (excluding IFI-financed projects) to 2% of GDP. It focuses exclusively on government debt and guarantees, excluding debt held by public enterprises.

Based on the latest DSA explained in the Economic Reform Programme (ERP) 2025-2027, the baseline scenario shows that the public debt stock will remain within manageable levels, with the debt-to-GDP ratio following a slight upward trend but not exceeding 25% by 2028. On the other hand, interest expenditures will remain low in the medium-term (2026-2028) while, financing needs will average around 3% of GDP reflecting the gradual reduction of the investment clause.

This DSA analysis is refrenced from the Economic Reform Programme (ERP) 2025-2027.

2.2.2. Fiscal Risks from Public Enterprises Publicly Owned Enterprises (POEs) may impose significant influence on fiscal outcomes, particularly when unexpected subsidies, loans, or capital injections (equity) become necessary, contingent liabilities are realized, or tax and dividend revenues fall short of projections. POEs indirectly affect fiscal indicators through their impact on economic growth. The likelihood of fiscal risks emerging from publicly owned companies increases when POEs are undercapitalized, operate at a loss, or face liquidity constraints.

In Kosovo, POEs are categorized in two groups: central and local government-owned. The central level includes 19 enterprises, 17 overseen by the Ministry of Economy, one (KOSTT)

by the Assembly, and one (Gjakova Airport) by the Kosovo Security Force (KSF). For the case of Trepça, its ownership is split, with the state holding 80% and workers 20%.

The following analysis is based on financial data compiled from the yearly audited reportsof these public enteprises which operate in various industries such as energy, transport, water supply, telecommunications and mining sector.

Kosovo’s POEs demonstrate relative financial stability, with total assets remaining steady at around 18.8% of GDP in 2024, reflecting a gradual decline over the past five years. Liabilities have also decreased notably, falling from 9.8% of GDP in 2020 to 7.1% in 2024, indicating some degree of deleveraging. Revenues peaked in 2022 representing 6.2% of GDP before declining to 3.9% in 2023 and slightly recovering to 4.3% of GDP in 2024. Equity levels remained stable overall, while profitability measures, such as Return on Assets and Return on Equity, showed significant volatility, with sharp drops between 2022 and 2023 followed by a strong recovery in 2024 to 3.6% and 5.8% respectively.

The electricity, gas and water utilities sectors continue to dominate the asset and revenue structure. However, the fluctuations in profitability and revenues highlight underlying vulnerabilities, suggesting the need for stronger governance and operational improvements to minimize fiscal risks.

Between 2022 and 2024, current and capital transfers showed notable shifts across sectors amounting to 0.14% of GDP by the end of year 2024. 2.2.3. Public Private Partnerships Kosovo’s Public-Private Partnership (PPP) portfolio remains relatively modest but it still demonstrates a significant contribution to the country’s infrastructure development.

Currently, Kosovo has three fully operational PPPs:

Additionally, there is another important project that is currently in the construction phase, which includes the development of three new schools with an investment cost of €16.6 million and a duration of 10 years. This project is contracted by the Municipality of Prishtina.

The total investment cost of the operational PPPs portfolio amounts to €129.4 million, representing 1.3% of Nominal GDP.

The level of risk of PPP projects depends on the contract type and risk-sharing structure outlined in the agreements. In Kosovo, PPP contracts are primarily concession-based, meaning the government bears no financial liability or capital investment. Instead, it generates revenue through concession fees paid by private entities. This structure minimizes fiscal risk, as the government benefits financially without upfront costs. However, concession fees are directly

tied to the financial performance of the project, which can be influenced by various external factors, including economic downturns and global crises.

PIA, the largest in Kosovo, assigns operational, financial, and demand risks mainly to the Private Partner. The government’s exposure is limited to Force Majeure, which may suspend obligations or, in prolonged cases, trigger contract termination, with compensation for insured losses. The COVID-19 pandemic prompted a 20-month contract extension to address financial impacts. Overall, the PPP model provides government benefits with minimal fiscal risk in case of no Force Majeure, though continued monitoring is essential.

2.2.4. Financial Sector Kosovo’s financial sector remains a critical pillar of economic stability and growth. Its effective operation is ensured through ongoing supervision by the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo (CBK), which publishes the Financial Stability Report annually. The most recent edition analyzes financial trends from January to December 2024 and outlines forward-looking risks into 2025.

This section of the report provides a comprehensive overview of the overall financial stability of the financial sector, assessing risks and sector performance. Compared to the previous FRS, this edition focuses in 2024 while extending into 2025 with a forward-looking perspective, deeper quantitative insights, and an expanded risk discussion.

The banking sector sustained a high lending pace in 2024, with overall credit growth at 18.3%, driven mainly by household loans, indicating a notable increase from 2023. Non-performing loans (NPL) ratios remained low at 1.9%, and deposits increased by 13.0%, continuing to serve as the sector’s main funding source. Accelerated lending growth offset the impact of changing interest rates, supporting net profit growth; however, further profit expansion faced a rise in interest expenses on deposits and intensifying competition for funds.

In 2024, household interest rates dropped to 6.1% for new consumer loans and 5.0% for new mortgage loans and corporate rates hit 6.4%. Despite liquidity imbalances between banks, overall sector liquidity stayed solid.

Pension funds saw strong asset growth due to positive developments in the international markets. The insurance sector continued to expand, supported mainly by the growth of nonlife segment premiums. Microfinance institutions remained at a high level of lending (24.6%), slightly lower than previous year, nevertheless increases in expenses resulted into slightly lower ROE and ROA, 13.3% and 3.6% respectively.

Commercial banks lead with €8.6 billion in assets and €182 million in profits, followed by pension funds (€3.2 billion), microfinance institutions (€651 million), and insurance firms (€334 million). ROEs are strong across sectors, ranging from 14.2% to 19.2%, while NPLs remain below 2.1%. Market concentration is high in banking and microfinance (over 52%), raising systemic risk concerns. Foreign ownership is also significant, especially in banking (83%). Overall, Kosovo’s financial system stayed resilient despite global and regional challenges. While some risks remain, its stability supports ongoing economic growth.

According to CBK’s monthly stability indicators (Jan–Aug 2025), the financial system continued to expand, driven by asset growth across commercial banks, microfinance institutions, insurance companies, and pension funds.

Commercial banks, the largest segment, maintained sound capitalization (CAR ~16.5%) and positive loan and deposit growth, but profitability declined, with average ROE falling to 18.4% (from 19.3% in 2024), and reaching 17.3% in August. Asset quality slightly weakened, as the NPL ratio rose to 2.1%. Microfinance institutions also expanded in loans and assets but saw ROE drop to 12.9% in August (Jan–Aug average: 13.1%, down from 14.6% in 2024), while NPLs averaged 1.8%. The pension sector showed strong asset growth, reaching €3,525 by August, and the insurance sector increased total assets to €355 million, with an average ROE of 16.9% and cumulative premiums of €120 million.

The figures show Kosovo’s banking sector is strong and resilient, outperforming the Western Balkans and Emerging Eurozone in key areas. ROE reached around 19.7% in 2024, and NPLs fell below 1.9%, indicating solid profitability and credit quality. However, the capital-to-riskweighted assets ratio, at about 17.4% in 2024, remains lower than the Eurozone and the Western Balkans, highlighting the need for prudent capital planning and supervisory.

Key Risks and Challenges Despite positive developments, Kosovo’s financial sector continues to face key risks, several of which are defined in CBK’s Financial Stability Report and presented below.

Interest rate risk, in Kosovo’s banking sector are rising, even though banks have benefited from higher rates via interest-bearing assets. This can be seen through a growing trend in fixed-rate lending (shifting risks to banks), the maturity gap widened (to 0.18% of equity), the liquidity

gap reaching €1,130.1 million in 2024. Funding costs and deposit competition are rising while deposit growth slows creating asset-liability mismatches, which results to profitability potentially being squeezed.

Geopolitical tensions around the globe, together with escalating trade frictions are the main constraints on the outlook. Particularly the US tariffs and broader trade fragmentation have raised market volatility, weakened confidence and slowed exports, hitting EU- linked economic like Kosovo. Although, it has not directly affected Kosovo’s banking system, it can push up energy-related inflation, unemployment and credit stress, making the financial system more vulnerable.

Climate change represents a broad financial threat, as both its physical and transition effects have the potential to destabilize the economy and financial system. The report highlights the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) as a new channel of risk for Kosovo:

about 34% of exports head to the EU, and emission-intensive sectors (base metals, cement)

could face higher costs and lost competitiveness. The banks direct exposure is small today, but those borrowers often provide collateral that could lose value if industrial activity slows, raising credit risk and the need for provisions.

Deposit insurance poses a financial risk for the government or central bank as Kosovo's limited coverage increases the risk of large withdrawals during financial crises. This scheme helps maintain trust by covering up to €5,000 per depositor, per bank, however, as the government guarantee phased out in December 2023, reliance on the fund’s own resources may raise concerns about its crisis capacity.

Source: The Kosovo Deposit Insurance Fund 2024 Report, MFTP calculations

Figure 13 shows that uninsured deposits make up the majority of total deposits in 2023 and 2024. While 99.9% of depositors are insured, with an average deposit of €4,446, they hold only 20% of total deposits. Insurance coverage exceeds the average deposit, but deposit concentration is assymetric. Although both insured and uninsured deposits are increasing, their share remains at around 13.8% and 53.7% of GDP, respectively. This highlights a

potential risk—in the event of a crisis, a large portion of deposits would not be covered, increasing the likelood of higher withdrawal rates and potential pressure on financial stability.

CBK stress tests show Kosovo’s Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) falls from 210.9% under baseline conditions to 96.3% in a severe scenario (23.8% withdrawals) and 87.4% in an extreme case (32.1% withdrawals), revealing clear vulnerability to large deposit outflows. If the LCR drops below regulatory limits5, financial stability could be endangered and emergency liquidity assistance or government support might be required. This underscores the need to strengthen the deposit-insurance and contingency framework to reduce fiscal risks and bolster depositor confidence.

Concluding Remarks This Fiscal Risk Statement provides a comprehensive overview of the key risks that could affect Kosovo’s fiscal outlook. By assessing macroeconomic uncertainties, fiscal performance and sector-specific exposures, ranging from public debt and guarantees to public enterprises, PPPs, and the financial sector, this report aims to inform more resilient and forward-looking fiscal planning. In doing so, it promotes transparency, strengthens fiscal discipline, and helps policymakers identify early warning signals that may require corrective action. The Statement also contributes to aligning fiscal risk management practices with international standards and reflects Kosovo’s commitment to sound economic governance.

Regulatory limit for LCR is set at 100%.
